headline: Friday is the warmest day of the stretch, with highs around 80 at the coast and in the 80s inland, before a cooling trend leads into a strong Pacific storm Tuesday and Wednesday that is very likely to bring 1 inch or more of rain from the coast to the mountains, plus strong winds and possible thunderstorms.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: High pressure overhead keeps the warming going Friday, with highs 12 to 18 degrees above average from the coast to the coastal mountain slopes: around 80 near the coast and in the 80s in the valleys and inland coastal areas. The lower deserts also reach the 80s, and the mountains run from the lower 60s to lower 80s. Skies stay mostly clear, with some high clouds moving in late Friday night.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Over the weekend the high pressure weakens and ocean breezes return and strengthen, so temperatures cool Saturday and Sunday while staying above average. By Sunday, highs at the coast and in the valleys are mostly in the 70s, around 80 in the lower deserts, and in the lower 50s to lower 70s in the mountains. Saturday morning's high clouds thin out Saturday afternoon into Sunday.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Clouds increase Sunday night and Monday with a chance of showers, though the chance of a quarter inch or more of rain through Monday afternoon stays below 25 percent. Rain chances rise Monday night ahead of a strong Pacific storm that arrives Tuesday, with the biggest impacts currently expected around Tuesday morning, bringing heavy rain, strong winds and a chance of thunderstorms. Through Wednesday night the chance of 1 inch or more of rain is above 90 percent from the coast to the mountains; the chance of 3 inches or more is 40 to 50 percent in far northern San Diego County (including the Carlsbad area) and 25 to 35 percent in far southern San Diego County, and in Orange and southwestern San Bernardino Counties it ranges from 35 to 45 percent near the coast to 60 to 70 percent in the mountains. Snow levels stay mostly above 8,000 feet through Tuesday, and rain tapers off Wednesday night and Thursday as the storm moves farther inland and east.

coast: Friday's 10 AM high tide is forecast around 7.6 to 7.7 feet, with tides running about a foot above normal predictions, so King Tides plus elevated surf bring moderate coastal flooding Friday morning under a Coastal Flood Warning for the Orange and San Diego County coasts until 1 PM Friday. A High Surf Advisory for San Diego County beaches runs until 4 AM Friday; a long-period west swell (7 to 9 feet every 16 to 18 seconds) has been producing 6 to 8 foot breakers with local 10 to 12 foot sets on exposed west-facing beaches, lowering Friday morning to 3 to 5 feet, with sets to 7 feet on Saturday. Minor coastal flooding is possible Saturday morning where surf is elevated (high tide near 7 feet), with high tides falling below 7 feet Sunday. No hazardous boating conditions are expected through Monday, but Tuesday's storm could bring gale-force winds over the coastal waters and high surf. Recent tides have set records: 4 of the 8 highest water levels ever measured at San Diego's Broadway Pier came this week, and the next King Tides peak around the morning high tide on December 24.
watch_for: Moderate coastal flooding around Friday's 10 AM King Tide, under a Coastal Flood Warning until 1 PM Friday

confidence: Confidence is high in the warm, dry weather through the weekend and very high that Tuesday–Wednesday's storm brings at least an inch of rain, while its exact timing and whether totals reach 3 inches or more remain uncertain.
